extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of pre-modern / medieval natural philosophy and experimental crafts (alchemy, distillation, metallurgy)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and interpreting the treatise's criteria about the nature, generation, extinction, taxonomy, and experimental production of heat/ignition and related processes (distillation, separation, purgation). The page is a Latin natural-philosophical/technical exposition on fire and caloric phenomena with experimental remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of ignis (fire)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignis nihil aliud est quam calor valde magnus cum siccitate iunctus. (Fire is nothing other than very great heat joined with dryness.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit statement that both a large degree of heat and dryness are jointly required for something to be called 'fire'. Heat alone (e.g., in water that is hot) does not constitute fire; dryness (siccitas) is a necessary constituent. The text uses this as a baseline criterion for identifying and reasoning about ignition and fire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of ignition (generation of fire)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propagatone, antipasis, percussione, frictione, putredine, coitione — the listed modes by which fire can be produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author enumerates principal ways fire may be produced: propagation, 'antipasis' (antiphasis/antispasis — joining/attraction?), percussion (blows), friction (rubbing), putrefaction, and coition (contact/joining). Explanatory notes: putrefaction alone may not suffice but can be confirmed or aided by heat; percussion and friction can generate heat if the motion/force is sufficiently concentrated; coition relates to bringing substances into contact in a way that concentrates heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignition by motion requires dryness
rubrics_metrics.description: Quod motu accenditur, siccum esse oportet — what is kindled by motion must be dry, not moist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If fire arises from motion (friction, percussion), the material must be dry; moist materials cannot be ignited by motion alone (they can be ignited only by existing fire). This is used as a diagnostic rule when deciding whether a given process can generate flame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thinness (tenuitas) and attenuation favor ignition
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials that are tenuous/attenuated and dry are most apt to take on igneous form; attenuation/separation promotes the reception/production of fire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thin, finely divided, or attenuated substances (pulvis, tenuia, capilli, spiritus-like parts) more readily become ignitable and take heat. Practical means of producing tenuity (grinding, pulverizing, distillation, separating parts) are described as ways to make otherwise non-ignitable materials yield fire or be consumed by fire. Opposite anti-pattern: gross, dense, humid materials resist ignition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion is the causal source of heat (calor as effect of motus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat is produced by motion; inquiry into how motion causes heat underlies explanations of ignition and increases of calor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues (and engages with Aristotelian positions) that motion is the cause of heat: introducing motion increases heat and thereby can produce fire. This functions as a theoretical criterion for explaining experimental observations (e.g., why friction and percussion produce heat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cold is the privation of heat
rubrics_metrics.description: Frigus nihil est prater caloris privationem — cold is nothing but the privation/absence of heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conceptual criterion reframes 'cold' as nonpositive (absence of calor) rather than a positive contrary substance. Consequence: cooling processes are understood as diminution/removal of motion/heat; explanations of rapid vs gradual cooling follow from this definition (e.g., how contact with cold bodies or removal of motion reduces heat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourfold taxonomy of calor (calor quadruplex)
rubrics_metrics.description: Calor quadruplex: (1) celestial/radiant heat (from stars), (2) igneous heat (fire-like, which causes separation and corrosion), (3) natural calor (requires motion; found in animals and living bodies), (4) vestigial trace/vestigium of heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each kind has distinct origins and effects: celestial heat is external and not generated in material; igneous heat acts to separate and corrump (corrupt) substances; natural calor is tied to internal motion and life; the 'vestige' is a remaining small warmth. This taxonomy is used as a diagnostic rubric for attributing observed heating effects to underlying sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition proportions determine combustibility and character
rubrics_metrics.description: The relative quantities of earth, water, air, and heat in a mixture decide whether it is terrestrial (resists fire), aqueous, or aerial and therefore more or less prone to be ignited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule of thumb: mixtures rich in earth resist ignition and motion; those with abundant air are more 'aerial' and readily take heat; oily/fatty substances (pingue) are easily ignited. Examples: pepper is not easily ignited because despite being light it contains much terrestrial substance; aggregates with more earth require greater effort to produce fire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical criteria for hidden fire in materials (stones etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tests for whether fire is contained in a material: does attrition produce sparks/flammation without consuming the substance? Does the material, when finely reduced, produce flame? Are vapors emitted when heated?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise uses experiments (rubbing stones, observing whether sparks or flames and whether the substance is consumed) to infer whether fire is 'hidden' in stones. Observed regularities: many hard stones need stronger percussion to produce sparks; in some cases very fine powder of a substance will ignite while the intact stone will not. The author concludes that fire is not inherently hidden in most stones but can be produced when their substance is reduced to finer parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of extinction: humidity and cold (and obstruction of 'respiration' / motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fire is extinguished by cold and by humid bodies because they (1) oppose the heat's contrary quality and (2) physically prevent the respiration/movement required for heat's activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twofold mechanism: (a) contrary quality (cold, moisture) counters and overcomes heat; (b) humid or cold surrounds inhibit the motions (or 'respiration') that sustain heat. Practical implication: water extinguishes fire not only by cooling but by impeding the processes that keep the material in a dry, motile condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental methods for distillation, separation and purification
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural guidance: use glass (vitreis) vessels, controlled heat, repeated distillation/collection of fractions (crocea etc.), use of alkaline/cinder additions (cineres, nitrum, alum, etc.) to separate metals or purify waters and oils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical notes: purity of starting material is crucial to avoid false results; fine control of heat and vessel sealing preserves volatile fractions; repeated distillations and the use of ash/alkalis aid in separating metallic impurities (e.g., silver from water). The text gives concrete experimental observations and cautions (e.g., some procedures require long heating, specific ashes, glassware).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of materials as criterion for valid distillation/chemical operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Material used for making distilled waters or 'aether' must be free of falsity/contamination; only pure matter will yield the expected product without false appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author insists on careful selection of feedstock (e.g., avoidance of adulterants) and notes that certain animal or plant wastes (e.g., pigeon dung, certain slags) have been used experimentally but must be handled with vigilance. This is a methodological rule for trustworthiness of outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particle size / substance fineness influences medicinal and erosive effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The fineness (tenuitas) or grossness (crassitudo) of a medicament affects its action: very fine substances act quickly and painfully (rapid erosion), moderate fineness is less painful but effective, gross and heavy substances act slowly and with less pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to therapeutics and cauterizing agents: finely reduced powders and preparations produce faster heating/erosion (useful for certain operations) but produce more pain; coarser preparations act more slowly with less pain. This provides a practical rubric for preparing formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire separates and mixes: criterion for cookery vs corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignis mixes and also separates (concoquit and corrumpit): it cooks food by separating parts, making some substances suitable as food while corrupting others; whether cooking increases longevity or not depends on use and habituation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a heuristic for judging culinary or preservative effects of heat: the same separating power that makes food digestible can also corrupt or diminish nutritive quality. The text uses this to evaluate when cooking is beneficial vs harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of retained 'vestige' of heat (veftigium) to lasting warmth
rubrics_metrics.description: Some materials retain a vestige or remainder of heat (veftigium) without retaining full calor; such residues can make e.g. lime remain warm for a time though cooled externally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between retaining the 'trace' of heat and retaining active calor. This criterion is used to explain why some substances remain warm internally after heating and why others (ashes) do not.
